The New General Service List (NGSL) has 2,809 lemmas that cover about 92% of general English. The New Academic Word List (NAWL) adds 959 lemmas for academic reading beyond the NGSL. Both are by Browne, Culligan & Phillips.
The PHRASE List’s own ratings for every expression found: how common each one is in speech, general writing and academic writing, compared with the other two.

The PHRASal Expressions List (Martinez & Schmitt 2012) holds the most frequent multiword expressions in English whose meaning is hard to work out from their words. It was compiled for teaching reading. Each expression is ranked in the same 1,000-item bands as the BNC word families, as if words and phrases formed one list, so in terms of, made of 1K words, is a 2K item. The list also rates how common each expression is in speech, general writing and academic writing. Matching follows inflections (dealt with), checks the grammar where senses differ (going to as future, not direction), and counts only the longest of overlapping expressions.

These are the counts every other measure is built on. A word is an orthographic word, so don’t, well-known and cannot are one word each. Numbers count as words for readability but are left out of type counts.

These formulas use surface features such as word and sentence length. Against teachers’ rankings of 4,724 school texts, they explain about a quarter to a third of the differences in difficulty (Crossley et al. 2023).

These indices measure how varied the vocabulary is. The simple type/token ratio falls as a text grows, so it cannot compare texts of different lengths. MTLD, HD-D and vocd-D were designed to avoid this.
These levels are not from the Cambridge English Vocabulary Profile. If you report them, cite CEFR-J and Octanove.

These measures follow Lu’s (2010) L2 Syntactic Complexity Analyzer (L2SCA): the length of sentences, T-units and clauses, how much subordination and coordination they carry, and how much is packed into noun phrases. A T-unit is a main clause with everything attached to it, so I left because it rained is one T-unit with two clauses.
They were normed on US native-speaker readers, and the evidence for language learners is thinner. For learners, check the vocabulary profile too.

lexinspect profiles English writing the way applied linguists do: readability by eight published formulas, vocabulary against CEFR-J, Nation’s BNC/COCA families, NGSL and the AWL, multiword expressions from Martinez & Schmitt’s PHRASE List, sentence complexity after Lu’s L2SCA, Hyland’s metadiscourse and a UK/US spell check. Every finding is marked where it occurs, with what to change for readers at a given CEFR level.
